To ease the financial burden of implementing a large-scale bike share system,
municipalities should begin with a smaller network and phase expansion in
response to demand. This approach helps prevent system sprawl and keeps
operating costs manageable.

Establishing a consistent station density throughout the service area builds user
confidence in the system, ensuring they will find a station or bike where ever they
may need to go.

National interviews revealed greater success in bike share adoption when
neighboring municipalities launched an integrated system in a coordinated effort.

Dockless systems have lower upfront capital costs, but operational costs tend to be
higher in comparison to docked stations. Riders and community members favor the
option of docking at stations to physically signify the end of a rental period. In the
Divvy system, docked e-bikes have higher ridership than dockless e-bikes.

Peer interviews saw success when new bike share services launched adjacent to
existing service boundaries, connecting communities and expanding the overall
footprint.

Interest in e-bikes is growing, as they increase accessibility and allow riders to
more easily take longer trips. Peer cities interviewed saw success with e-bikes
making up 30% to 50% of their system.

Bike share station ridership tends to be highest when placed in areas with a
concentration of active, mixed land uses and transit, allowing users to conveniently
access a range of destinations and services.
